query: Which eigenvector/eigenvalue conventions (adjacency vs Laplacian, normalized vs unnormalized, left vs right, sign) should be the default and how must degeneracies be handled programmatically?

response.query: Which eigenvector/eigenvalue conventions (adjacency vs Laplacian, normalized vs unnormalized, left vs right, sign) should be the default and how must degeneracies be handled programmatically?
response.answer: Default convention: use unnormalized Laplacian eigenvectors. Handle degeneracies by selecting one eigenvector per eigenvalue.

results.content: # How to prove that the Laplacian for a directed graph has an eigenvalue at 0? Modified 5 years, 11 months ago If Laplacian L = D-A where D is the degree matrix and A is an 0-1 adjacency matrix for a directed graph. How can we prove that this Laplacian has an eigenvalue at 0? asked Oct 6, 2019 at 21:02 21922 silver badges99 bronze badges ## 1 Answer 1 Let $\textbf{1}$ be the function taking the value $1$ at each vertex. Consequently, $$ (D-A)\textbf{1}=0, $$ which means that $\textbf{1}$ is an eigenvector of the Laplacian with eigenvalue $0$. 2019-10-07 05:32:14 +00:00 Commented Oct 7, 2019 at 5:32 * $\begingroup$ @m1cro1ce none of those results are necessary just to prove that $0$ is an eigenvalue of the Laplacian. 2019-10-07 06:37:30 +00:00 Commented Oct 7, 2019 at 6:37 * $\begingroup$ One doubt would be how is $A\textbf{1} = deg(v)$? Because $A\textbf{1}$ will give us only the in-degree for every node in the network while $deg(v)$ is the sum of both in-degree and out-degree at a node in a directed graph right? But it is not the sum, it must be one or the other (whichever matches the convention used for the adjacency matrix: if $A\_{ij}$ is directed edge from $i$ to $j$, or from $j$ to $i$.) results.title: While doing spectral clustering, why do we find the eigenvector of the graph Laplacian? Why not use adjacency matrix directly? - Quora
results.content: While doing spectral clustering, why do we find the eigenvector of the graph Laplacian? Spectral clustering uses the eigenvectors of a graph Laplacian because the Laplacian encodes global connectivity and cluster-smoothness properties that are aligned with the clustering objective; the adjacency matrix does not provide the same spectral relationship to graph cuts and diffusion. Spectral clustering uses the eigenvectors of a graph Laplacian because the Laplacian encodes global connectivity and cluster-smoothness properties that are aligned with the clustering objective; the adjacency matrix does not provide the same spectral relationship to graph cuts and diffusion. * Stability and ordering: Laplacian eigenvalues are nonnegative and the multiplicity of the zero eigenvalue equals number of connected components; small nonzero eigenvalues indicate near-separated clusters and give a clear ordering for selecting eigenvectors. * Community detection alternatives: in some regimes (e.g., stochastic block models with certain parameters), leading eigenvectors of suitably regularized or normalized adjacency matrices (e.g., A − α11^T, non-backtracking matrix, Bethe Hessian) work well and can even outperform raw Laplacian methods. where L denotes the normalized Laplacian matrix of a graph, and the solution is the eigenvector corresponding to the second smallest eigenvalue of L, since the smallest. results.content: Stack Exchange network consists of 183 Q&A communities including Stack Overflow, the largest, most trusted online community for developers to learn, share their knowledge, and build their careers. # Null space squared Laplacian matrix. I have a matrix $G$ that is a row-normalized adjacency matrix of a connected graph. From the Perron-Frobenius theorem, I know that $G$ has a unique (largest) eigenvalue 1 (the eigenvector is the vector of ones). Therefore, I know that the Laplacian matrix $(I-G)$ has a unique eigenvalue 0 (the eigenvector is again the vector of ones), so the null space of $(I-G)$ is of dimension 1 and is proportional to this vector of ones. Now my question is how to prove that the null space of $(I-G)^2$ is also of dimension 1 (and not of 2). edited Jun 16, 2021 at 10:43. asked Jun 16, 2021 at 10:37. * $\begingroup$ If this is an undirected graph, then $(I - G)$ is symmetric. Applying this with $A = I-G$ gives you the result you're after $\endgroup$. $\begingroup$ If this is a directed graph: the Perron-Frobenius theorem also tells you that $1$ will be a *simple* eigenvalue of $G$, which is to say that the algebraic multiplicity will be $1$. It follows that $(I - G)$ and $(I - G)^2$ have the same null space dimension. How do you conclude that $(I-G)$ and $(I-G)^2$ have the same null space dimension from the algebraic multiplicity of 1? $\begingroup$ The algebraic multiplicity of $1$ is the maximum dimension of the null space of $(I - G)^k$ for all integers $k \geq 0$.
